evidence_works.detail: The paper takes Helimski's description (final CVV syllable stressed, otherwise the penult; secondary stress on heavy syllables and alternate light syllables) and adds the sonority effect: in light trisyllables main stress optionally moves to an antepenult with [a e o] when the penult has [i y u ə ɨ], never further left, and rarely in four-syllable words, with mid and low vowels treated alike and high peripheral and central vowels treated alike. It also reports that stressed vowels are longer and louder, and that the two vowel classes do not differ in duration, so the effect is sonority, not vo

Heavy syllables (codas and/or long vowels) 'do not attract primary stress away from initial position' (ex. 2778.srule: Monomorphemic words: secondary stresses on every other syllable after the initial primary stress, left to right (binary trochees, e.g. (pára)(càɻu) 'thirsty'); never on a word-final syllable, an odd final syllable left unfooted ((ŋáɻi)ri 'bank'). Heavy syllables (coda and/or long vowel) may optionally form their own foot, so a secondary can fall on the next syllable ((wúr)(kàɻu) 'three', (ɻáː)(kàra) 'morning'). Polymorphemic words: feet align with morphemes; secondary stresses on the initial syllables of disyllabic or longer morphemes, monomoraic suffixes/enclitics footed together ((cúŋa=l)(kù=lu)); in preverb + verb complex verbs the verb root's first syllable takes a secondary stress, clash permitted ((cáː)=(kàri)-ja). 2783.prule: Non-phonemic (phonetic) word stress assigned by a ranked hierarchy of syllable types: (1) a syllable with a phonetically lengthened vowel -- i.e. a full vowel /i e a o u/ non-final in the rhythm group and not before a semivowel, since full vowels are long there and short rhythm-group-finally, and /ə/ is never lengthened -- outranks (2) an open word-final full-vowel syllable, which outranks (3) a non-final schwa syllable, which outranks (4) an open word-final schwa syllable. In the (all disyllabic) examples this gives initial stress when the first syllable has a full vowel ([ˈŋaːkːo]) or both syllables have schwa ([ˈŋəgə], [ˈdəndə]) and final stress when only the final has a full vowel ([rəˈgo]). No edge, window or tie-break among several lengthened vowels is stated; secondary stress not discussed.

tn.translation: The tone language (molàpo a imbóyidi) ... is based on the presence of lexical tones. ... In this case every vowel, every syllable, has a definite tone, which has the high tone level and the low tone level, and the tones have phonological value, i.e. there are minimal pairs of words with different meanings that differ only in their tones. ... In Ndowé, since different tones are used for one and the same word, there are also several accents without any one syllabic unit being singled out above the others of the word or phonic group.

2789.prule: A stress accent ('accent d'intensité') on the first syllable of the radical (stem-initial); the second stem syllable and the prefixes (*NV-) are unstressed. Since native Engungwel radicals are synchronically monosyllabic (CV, CVV, CVC, CVVC, CVVV; sec. 2.4 p. 66), the stress falls on the single radical syllable of a prefix+radical word. Position is fixed by morphology (the stem), not by word edge or syllable count.
2789.srule: Echo (secondary) prominence on the third syllable of the radical, two syllables after the stem-initial primary, with the second syllable and the prefixes unstressed — Paulian (1994: 121-122) as relayed and tentatively adopted by Raharimanantsoa ('un accent d'intensité réalisé sur la première syllabe du radical, qui trouve son écho dans la troisième syllabe'). Stated for trisyllabic radicals; native Engungwel radicals are synchronically monosyllabic (sec. 2.4 p. 66), so ordinary prefix+radical words have no syllable for the echo; nothing is said about reduplicated, compound or borrowed words, and no phonetic evidence is given.

tn.translation: As for the tones on the vowels, we observe that the same tonal patterns on radicals exist in Engungwel as in Kukuya (Hyman 1984: 311, 313): high (H), low (B), high-low (HB), low-high (BH) and low-high-low (BHB). Each vowel in Engungwel can thus carry an H tone, a B (low) tone or a modulated tone (HB, BH or even BHB), but the modulated tones are often realised over two or three vowels.

2790.tone: Lexical tone system: 6 tones on open/sonorant-final syllables in two registers (odd = high/first register, even = low/second register; categories A (1,2), B (3,4), C (5,6)) plus 2 tones (7, 8) on stop-final syllables = 8 tones, for both the Cổ Liêm and Yên Thọ dialects. Phonetic realisation differs from Vietnamese (low-series tones 2 and 4 start higher than 1 and 3; tones 3 and 4 glottalized; tones 4 and 6 often hard to distinguish; speakers often substitute Vietnamese tones in code-mixed speech, notated e.g. den2'). 2791.prule: No contrastive tone and no stress rule: every word carries one predictable H tone (the syllable of highest prominence). In inflected verbs the H sits on a TAM marker or on the stem-initial syllable, placed morphologically. In infinitives and nouns the H is placed by syllable weight: on the heavy (long-vowel, incl. conditioned-length) stem syllable, on the second when both the first and second stem syllables are heavy (in consonant-initial quadrisyllabic stems the H never falls later than the second stem syllable: a heavy third syllable puts it on the second); with no heavy syllable, trisyllabic stems take stem-final H (optionally spreading to the penult or whole stem), bisyllabic and consonant-initial quadrisyllabic stems take stem-initial H, monosyllabic stems carry H; vowel-initial trisyllabic stems take H on the last syllable unless the second is heavy; vowel-initial quadrisyllabic stems are mostly ØHØØ (never H on the prefix-shared initial syllable), some stems in -ɛɛɾ/-ɛɛr taking H on the heavy penult or on both the second syllable and the penult.

2796.dq: Sentence stress is as irregular as word stress. Independent personal pronouns are always stressed, whereby the immediately preceding verb loses its stress if it has less than two unstressed syllables between its last potentially stressed syllable and the pronoun ... The texts and examples in the grammar are written in orthography based on ideal sounds, not in transcription; hence the stress marks…
2796.dloc: Uldall 1954, section 6 'Stress', pp. 13-14 (archive.org issue scan). Shipley 1961 pp. 46, 49.
2796.prule: No fixed rule: 'No definite rule can be given as to the place of the stress in words and sentences, the best that can be done is to indicate tendencies.' Stress is non-contrastive (no minimal pairs). Tendencies are keyed to morphology, not syllable count or weight: nouns normally stress the last syllable, suffixes included (ki'le, hu:'k'-u-m), with many lexical exceptions ('maydik); verbs stress the syllable immediately before the tense suffix (he'nim-wesi, henim-'ti-wesi), except that the present-tense suffix syllable itself is stressed (so'l-i-m); verbalizing and nominalizing suffixes usually take the stress (kile-'pe, wo:nti-'hi) but -yu does not ('tuy-yu); imperative and subjunctive forms are final-stressed except second-person forms.
2796.srule: No graded or rhythmic secondary stress described; a second ('double') stress arises only from morphology: compound verbs may stress each stem or only one ('The latter seems to be the more common procedure'); occasionally a stem keeps its stress before a stressed derivative suffix (i'da:-'ti-t'omatoy); some nouns take a 'double stress' with case endings (oko'peype'y-i-m).
2796.quote: Stress does not seem to have any semantic or grammatical function, it has not been possible to find any pair of words distinguished by stress alone. No definite rule can be given as to the place of the stress in words and sentences, the best that can be done is to indicate tendencies. 2797.heavy: Syllables with tense (full) vowels bear the accent; 'Les voyelles non-tendues ne sont jamais accentuées en débit normal' -- non-tense/reduced vowels ([ə] and lax realizations of final vowels) never do. 2797.dflt: not stated; the case of a polysyllable with no eligible (full-vowel) non-final syllable is not discussed (all examples have one, always the stem-initial syllable)
2797.prule: A phonetic intensity accent, non-contrastive and (per the author) fully predictable; the phonology proper is tonal (H/B tonemes). Non-tense (lax/reduced, [ə]) vowels are never accented at normal tempo; monosyllables are unaccented except utterance-finally; disyllables: either syllable (subject to the lax-vowel ban); trisyllables: almost always the 2nd syllable whatever the tone pattern; longer words (offered tentatively): final vowel excluded, the first syllable counting from the right whose vowel is not [ə] (when the final vowel is not [i]), or the first syllable from the right whose vowel is not [i] (when the final vowel is [i]). Every underlined example places the accent on the stem-initial (radical) syllable: lə̀[bà]xə̀là, m'ɛ̀:[sá:]dá, [mwɛ̂:]nɛ̀, m'ɛ̀kà:[só]tə̀xà, ù[tsá]mə̀nà, àmá[ná:]mbə̀nà, ì[pé]pìdì, à[lì:]dì.
2797.srule: None at word level; only pause-conditioned: a syllable bearing the lowered (abaissé) tone before an utterance-internal (non-final) pause automatically takes an intensity accent, so such a word has its 'primaire' accent in the usual place plus a 'secondaire' on the lowered-tone syllable ('il y aura deux accents d'intensité, "primaire", là où il apparaît de toute façon dans le mot, et "secondaire" qui comprend le ton abaissé'). No rhythmic/alternating secondary stress is described.

tn.quote: L'analyse tonologique fait apparaître un tonème haut (H) et un tonème bas (B); chaque phonème vocalique porte obligatoirement un tonème quelconque ou une séquence de tonèmes: B + H ou H + B. L'identité phonologique des tonèmes simples ressort des paires minimales suivantes: /asagela/ "il défrichait' /asâgala/ 'qu'il défriche" /utsoka/ "laver" /utsôka/ "remuer" … l'apparition de tons modulés est imprévisible dans de nombreux énoncés, nous avons, par conséquent, été conduite à poser comme phonologique la séquence de tonèmes, malgré l'absence de paires minimales canoniques.
tn.translation: The tonological analysis brings out a high toneme (H) and a low toneme (B); every vowel phoneme obligatorily bears some toneme or a sequence of tonemes: L+H or H+L. The phonological identity of the simple tonemes emerges from the following minimal pairs: /asagela/ 'he was clearing (land)' /asâgala/ 'let him clear'; /utsoka/ 'wash' /utsôka/ 'stir' … the appearance of contour tones is unpredictable in many utterances, so we have consequently been led to posit the sequence of tonemes as phonological, despite the absence of canonical minimal pairs.

2798.prule: No word-stress rule is stated for N'Ko. The written norm is described purely as a tone language: every vowel is short or long, oral or nasal, and bears one of four tones (high, low, rising, word-final 'floating' low = tonal article), tone and length being obligatorily written with seven superscript diacritics (kánmasere). At family level Vydrin 2017: 34 states that stress is absent in most Mande languages and that where it can be identified (notably Bamana, as foot stress) its functional load is small.

2798.tone: Every N'Ko-specific source opened (Vydrin & Rovenchak 2017: 1104-1105; Rovenchak 2011: 85, 91-92; Diané & Vydrin 2014 sec. 3; Vydrin et al. 2016 'In N'ko, tonal marking is obligatory on every vowel'; Everson et al. 2004: 4-5; Donaldson 2017: 96, 138-139, 149-151; Vydrin 2012) characterises the norm by a four-tone system (H, L, rising, H + floating L) crossed with a length contrast, written obligatorily; none mentions stress, accent or prominence (the only 'stress' hit in the N'Ko texts is Rovenchak's aside on Classical Latin, p. 87, and 'accent aigu/grave' as diacritic names). The sole explicit stress statement is family-level (Vydrin 2017: 34): stress is absent in most Mande languages; where identifiable (Bamana, foot stress) its functional load is small.
2798.sec_loc: Vydrin & Rovenchak 2017 pp. 1103-1106 (N'Ko alphabet section); Vydrin 2017 pp. 33-34 (family prosody); Davydov 2017 pp. 164-171 (whole chapter); Rovenchak 2011 (whole article); Diané & Vydrin 2014 (whole article). No secondary or rhythmic stress is described for N'Ko/Maninka; the only related passages are Vydrin 2017 p. 34 (the foot as a rhythmic unit, with foot stress named only for Bamana) and Rovenchak 2011 p. 87 (an aside on stress rules in Classical Latin) and p. 88 (verse metre of traditional Maninka poetry).
